weber1998.title: A Quantitative Analysis and Performance Study for Similarity-Search Methods in High-Dimensional Spaces
weber1998.author: Roger Weber, Hans-J. Schek, Stephen Blott
weber1998.venue: Proceedings of the 24th VLDB Conference, New York, USA, 1998, pp. 194-205. Byline reads "Roger Weber / Institute of Information Systems / ETH Zentrum, 8092 Zurich", "Hans-J. Schek / Institute of Information Systems / ETH Zentrum, 8092 Zurich", "Stephen Blott / Bell Laboratories (Lucent Technologies) / 700 Mountain Ave, Murray Hill". Page footers run 194 to 205 across a 12-page scan.
weber1998.quote: We show formally that these methods exhibit linear complexity at high dimensionality, and that existing methods are outperformed on average by a simple sequential scan if the number of dimensions exceeds around 10.
quotes: We show formally that these methods exhibit linear complexity at high dimensionality, and that existing methods are outperformed on average by a simple sequential scan if the number of dimensions exceeds around 10.
Consequently, we come up with an alternative organization based on approximations to make the unavoidable sequential scan as fast as possible.
We describe a simple vector approximation scheme, called VA-file, and report on an experimental evaluation of this and of two tree-based index methods (an R*-tree and an X-tree).
Given this analytical and practical basis, we postulate that all approaches to nearest-neighbor search in HDVSs ultimately become linear at high dimensionality.
Further, we have shown that any partitioning scheme and clustering technique must degenerate to a sequential scan through all their blocks if the number of dimension is sufficiently large.

Experiments with synthetic and real data have shown that the performance of R*-trees and X-trees follows our analytical prediction, and that these tree-base structures are outperformed by a sequential scan by orders of magnitude if dimensionality becomes large.
We have shown that these methods are out-performed by a simple sequential scan at moderate dimensionality (i.e. d = 10).
In this section, therefore, we describe a simple method which accelerates that unavoidable scan by using object approximations to compress the vector data.

Depending upon the accuracy of the data points and the number of bits chosen, the approximation file is 4 to 8 times smaller than the vector file. Thus, storage overhead ratio is very small, on the order of 0.125 to 0.25.
For each dimension i, a small number of bits (bi) is assigned (bi is typically between 4 and 8), and 2^bi slices along the dimension i are determined in such a way that all slices are equally full.
Nearest neighbor queries are performed by scanning the entire approximation file, and by excluding the vast majority of vectors from the search (filtering step) based only on these approximations.
The VA-File is the only method which we have studied for which performance can even improve as dimensionality increases.
the VA-file offers the best performance in practice whenever the number of dimensions is larger than around 6

Space-partitioning methods like grid-file [27], K-D-B-tree [28] or quadtree [18] divide the data space along predefined or predetermined lines regardless of data clusters. Data-partitioning index trees such as R-tree [21], R+-tree [30], R*-tree [2], X-tree [7], SR-tree [24], M-tree [10], TV-tree [25] or hB-tree [26] divide the data space according to the distribution of data objects inserted or loaded into the tree.
In practice, based on our 20% threshold, the performance of these data-partitioning methods becomes worse than that of a simple scan if dimensionality exceeds 10.
A newer approach treats five overlapping parts of images separately, and generates a 45-dimensional feature vector for each image.
Figure 16: Wall-clock time for the image database.
N=50'000, image database, k=10
our results indicate that, even in the average case, nearest-neighbor searches ultimately access all data blocks as dimensionality increases
[34] R. Weber and S. Blott. An approximation based data structure for similarity search. Technical Report 24, ESPRIT project HERMES (no. 9141), October 1997.
Proceedings of the 24th VLDB Conference New York, USA, 1998
We only sketch the method here, and present the most relevant performance measurements.

In low-dimensional data spaces, the sequential scan (5 <= d <= 6) and the X-tree (d < 5) produce least disk operation and execute the nearest neighbor search fastest. In high-dimensional data spaces, that is d > 6, the VA-File outperforms all other methods.
The color similarity measure described by Stricker and Orengo [32] generates 9-dimensional feature vectors for each image.
Section 4 sketches the VA-File, and provides a performance evaluation of four methods.
Under the assumption of uniformity and independence, we have established lower bounds on the average performance of NN-search for space- and data-partitioning, and clustering structures.
While Hellerstein et al. have established worst-case results, ours is an average-case analysis.
the VA-File benefits from the sparseness of HDVS as opposed to partitioning or clustering methods
the number of cells (2^b) is much larger than the number of vectors (N) such that the vast majority of the cells must be empty

Observation 1 (Number of partitions) The most simple partitioning scheme splits the data space in each dimension into two halves. With d dimensions, there are 2^d partitions. With d <= 10 and N on the order of 10^6, such a partitioning makes sense. However, if d is larger, say d = 100, there are around 10^30 partitions for only 10^6 points - the overwhelming majority of the partitions are empty.
Hence, we consider an index structure to work 'well' if, on average, less than 20% of blocks must be visited, and to 'fail' if, on average, more than 20% of blocks must be visited.
Although a factor of 10 for this phenomenon is frequently assumed elsewhere (and was observed in our own PC and workstation environments), we assume a more conservative factor of only 5 here.
weber1998.note: Read as the scanned PDF at vldb.org, text extracted with pdftotext -layout. The scan's OCR is noisy in a consistent way: it substitutes commas inside words ("t,he", "best,"), reads the digit 8 as the letter S ("bi is typically between 4 and S"), mangles bracketed reference numbers ("[a]" for "[2]", "[lo]" for "[10]", "[la]" for "[12]", "[341" for "[34]"), drops superscripts (2^bi prints as "2b\""), and breaks lines across the two-column layout. Every quote above has had those OCR artifacts repaired and line breaks joined; wording, numbers and punctuation are otherwise as printed. Two OCR-visible oddities in the source itself are left alone and are the paper's own: "the number of dimension is sufficiently large" (singular) and "tree-base structures" in the conclusion. The low-dimensional crossover sentence OCRs its inequalities as '(5 2 d 2 6)'; restored to '(5 <= d <= 6)' above, which is the only reading consistent with the adjacent '(d < 5)' and 'd > 6'.

beyer1999.title: When Is "Nearest Neighbor" Meaningful?
beyer1999.author: Kevin Beyer, Jonathan Goldstein, Raghu Ramakrishnan, Uri Shaft
beyer1999.venue: ICDT'99, LNCS 1540, pp. 217-235. The paper's own first-page footer reads "Catriel Beeri, Peter Buneman (Eds.): ICDT'99, LNCS 1540, pp. 217-235, 1998." with a Springer copyright line dated 1998; DBLP records the conference as ICDT 1999, pages 217-235, DOI 10.1007/3-540-49257-7_15. Authors' affiliation as printed: "CS Dept., University of Wisconsin-Madison, 1210 W. Dayton St., Madison, WI 53706".
beyer1999.quote: We show that under a broad set of conditions (much broader than independent and identically distributed dimensions), as dimensionality increases, the distance to the nearest data point approaches the distance to the farthest data point.
quotes: We show that under a broad set of conditions (much broader than independent and identically distributed dimensions), as dimensionality increases, the distance to the nearest data point approaches the distance to the farthest data point.
To provide a practical perspective, we present empirical results on both real and synthetic data sets that demonstrate that this effect can occur for as few as 10-15 dimensions.
In particular, most such techniques proposed in the literature are not evaluated versus simple linear scan, and are evaluated over workloads for which nearest neighbor is not meaningful.
Often, even the reported experiments, when analyzed carefully, show that linear scan would outperform the techniques being proposed on the workloads studied in high (10-15) dimensionality!
beyer1999.note: The printed footer's "1998" is the Springer copyright year on the LNCS volume; the conference is ICDT 1999 (Jerusalem, January 1999) and the year recorded here is 1999, matching DBLP. The prose's only dated claim from this source is relative - "The year after", i.e. after Weber, Schek and Blott at VLDB in August 1998 - which holds against the conference date and against DBLP, not against the volume's 1998 copyright line.
supports: distance concentration: nearest and farthest neighbour distances converge as dimensionality grows
the effect shows up at as few as 10-15 dimensions on real data
the companion complaint that high-dimensional index papers were not being benchmarked against linear scan

indyk1998.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbors: Towards Removing the Curse of Dimensionality
indyk1998.author: Piotr Indyk, Rajeev Motwani
indyk1998.venue: STOC 1998, pp. 604-613 (DBLP). Byline as printed: "PIOTR INDYK, RAJEEV MOTWANI, Department of Computer Science, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305".
indyk1998.quote: Despite decades of effort, the current solutions are far from satisfactory; in fact, for large d, in theory or in practice, they provide little improvement over the brute-force algorithm which compares the query point to each data point.
quotes: Despite decades of effort, the current solutions are far from satisfactory; in fact, for large d, in theory or in practice, they provide little improvement over the brute-force algorithm which compares the query point to each data point.

Of late, there has been some interest in the approximate nearest neighbors problem, which is: Find a point p in P that is an e-approximate nearest neighbor of the query q in that for all p' in P, d(p, q) <= (1 + e)d(p', q).
The problem was originally posed in the 1960s by Minsky and Papert [53, pp. 222-225], and despite decades of effort the current solutions are far from satisfactory.
Its key ingredient is the notion of locality-sensitive hashing
4.2 Locality-Sensitive Hashing
indyk1998.note: Read as a scanned PDF; OCR substitutes commas inside words and mangles the Greek epsilon, rendered here as 'e'. Wording and numbers otherwise as printed. Published the same year as Weber, Schek and Blott and independently of it; no causal link between the two is claimed anywhere in the prose or on a card.
supports: locality-sensitive hashing and the approximate-nearest-neighbour formulation arrived in 1998, the same year as the VLDB analysis
theoreticians had independently reached the same floor: for large d, exact methods barely beat brute force
locality-sensitive hashing is named in this paper as its key ingredient

unverified: Any figure in real currency. The paper's funding lines name 'the European ESPRIT project HERMES (project no. 9141)' and 'Swiss Bundesamt fur Bildung und Wissenschaft (BBW, grant no. 93.0135)' but publish no amount; the CORDIS record for project id 9141 returns HTTP 404. No money figure appears in the prose, so O9's cost is carried as the decade of tree indexes invalidated and the 4-to-8x ceiling on the VA-File, not as a currency amount.

The claim that Weber, Schek and Blott 'set out to build a better index' as a stated motivation. The paper never says so. What is verifiable is that the VA-File already existed as Technical Report 24 of ESPRIT project HERMES in October 1997, dated in the VLDB paper's own reference list, and the VLDB 1998 paper is the analysis published after it. The prose states only that ordering.

The contents of Weber and Blott, Technical Report 24, ESPRIT project HERMES, October 1997. Only its reference-list entry in the VLDB paper was opened; the report itself was not, so nothing is attributed to it beyond its title and date.

That the VLDB 1998 result caused multidimensional-index research to stop. The end of the R*-tree / X-tree / SS-tree / SR-tree line and the turn to approximation is a widely repeated reading with no source opened for it, so the prose claims only what the paper claims about those two trees in its own experiments.

That today's ANN benchmarks report against brute-force scan because of this paper. The practice is real and the chapter relies on it, but no source establishing the lineage was opened, so the ripple card states the shape of the result, not its citation history.

The full form of Hans-J. Schek's given name as the paper prints it. The byline gives only the initial; DBLP records the author as Hans-Jorg Schek. The initialled form as printed is used everywhere here.

Whether Weber, Schek and Blott lacked comparative evidence for the VA-File before the VLDB analysis. Technical Report 24 (October 1997) was not opened, so nothing can be said about what it did or did not measure. A prose clause asserting they 'had no evidence anyone should prefer it' was removed on verification; only the ordering of the two documents remains in the prose.

That the authors ever called the VA-File an index and then stopped. The VLDB paper calls it 'a simple vector approximation scheme' and 'an alternative organization based on approximations', and reserves 'index methods' for the R*-tree and X-tree; the October 1997 report is titled 'An approximation based data structure for similarity search'. No renaming is evidenced, so the prose now states only that the thing is not an index.

That Indyk and Motwani originated approximate nearest neighbour search. Their own abstract says 'Of late, there has been some interest in the approximate nearest neighbors problem' and their results 'significantly improve the known bounds', so the ripple card claims only that they paved a road that already existed, with locality-sensitive hashing as the named key ingredient.
